name: Made-in-India Shipping Containers: CMPS Scheme & Import Substitution
scope: India's Rs 10,000 cr Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme (Cabinet-approved 28 Oct 2026), the import-substitution gap versus China, and which Indian listed companies have confirmed (vs loosely attributed) container exposure.

summary.one_line: The Cabinet has approved a Rs 10,000 cr, 13-year subsidy to build Indian container capacity close to 7.5 lakh TEU from roughly 24,000 TEU of actual output, but listed exposure is thin: Kalyani Cast-Tech is the only pure-play, and its stock has already rerated about 2.6x off its low. Scheme guidelines, sanctioned plants and firm orders are all still to come.
key_points: On 28 Oct 2026 the Union Cabinet approved the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme (CMPS) with Rs 10,000 cr outlay up to FY2039-40. It has three costed components: Rs 8,891 cr operational-expenditure assistance per container sold, Rs 859 cr for 3% p.a. interest subvention on term loans, and Rs 150 cr for common testing and certification (S1, S2).

Eligibility (as reported, not in the Cabinet release text): new plants need at least 1 lakh TEU/yr and expansions must add at least 25,000 TEU, with commissioning within three years of in-principle approval (S1, S4).

One report says support is Rs 49,500 per 20ft and Rs 86,625 per 40ft box, with at least 70% local content until FY32 rising to 90% from FY33 (S3). We found only this one source for these figures, so treat them as provisional until guidelines are notified.

India imports nearly 2 million empty containers a year against a recorded maximum domestic output of about 24,000 TEU in FY2024, roughly 1.2% of need (S5, S23). The Core cites about 70,000 units of installed capacity but output near 25,000 (S6).

Indian boxes cost an estimated $500-1,000 (30-40%) more than Chinese ones (S6, S7). Corten steel is about 60-65% of cost and Indian corten runs 10-15% dearer (S6). On those figures the reported Rs 86,625 support per 40ft box (S3) is roughly the top end, about $1,000, of the estimated gap (our arithmetic, at about Rs 85-90/$).

Confirmed listed exposure is narrow. Kalyani Cast-Tech (market cap about Rs 828 cr) has built 13,000+ boxes since 2021 and lists 10,000 TEU/yr container capacity at Shivlakha, Kutch (S11, S12, S13). DCM Shriram built Maersk's first India-made EXIM box but on 6 Jul 2026 denied a reported 1,000-unit order (S8, S10). Mazagon Dock's only known container work is a 2022 CONCOR order for 2,500 boxes worth about Rs 100 cr (S15).

The market has partly priced it in: Kalyani trades at Rs 1,153 against a range of Rs 439-1,404 (S11). DCM Shriram (Rs 912, range Rs 886-1,356) and Mazagon Dock (Rs 1,733, range Rs 1,688-2,848) sit near their lows, which reflects their core businesses, not containers (S20, S21).

for_investors.title: Who benefits
points: Kalyani Cast-Tech is the only listed company where containers are core. It has a 10,000 TEU/yr unit, a Rs 133 cr order book and a reefer technology tie-up with a Japanese partner (S13). To reach the 25,000 TEU brownfield threshold it would need roughly 2.5x its current capacity (our arithmetic, S4, S13).

DCM Shriram has a proven ISO 1496-tested EXIM prototype accepted by Maersk (S24). If it commits scheme-scale capex, it has the balance sheet to qualify. On Rs 13,538 cr FY26 revenue (S20), containers would still be a small line.
CONCOR, as a box buyer, and shipping lines such as Maersk, which needs 400,000-500,000 boxes a year globally (S8), gain a second source if Indian prices close the gap.

for_investors.title: Who is hurt / risks
points: Subsidy dependence: experts quoted by The Core warn of a scale paradox (scale is needed to cut cost, and low cost is needed to win scale) and say China could cut prices further (S6).
Corten steel localisation is the binding constraint. Specialised weathering steel is well under 1% of India's crude steel output (S6), which makes a 70-90% local-content rule hard to meet (S3).

Small and mid caps named in Feb 2026 'container stocks' lists mostly have wagon, logistics or construction exposure, not box-making (S17, S18). Trans Freight Containers has ceased manufacturing altogether (S19).

for_investors.title: What to watch
points: Notification of CMPS guidelines: per-unit rates, local-content rules and the approval process. The Cabinet release did not state per-container rates or a guideline date (S4).
The first in-principle approvals and any exchange filing or board approval for a 1 lakh TEU greenfield plant. None was found as of 29 Oct 2026.
Whether Maersk's 1,000-unit order is formalised with DCM Shriram (S8, S10), and any new CONCOR container tenders.
Kalyani's Q2 FY27 results and capex disclosure for container capacity (S13).

kpis.sub: Cabinet approval 28 Oct 2026, up to FY2039-40 (S1, S2)

sections.title: Theme explainer: why India wants to make its own boxes

blocks.text: India imports nearly 2 million empty containers a year (S5, S23). Maximum domestic production was about 24,000 TEU in FY2024, roughly 1.2% of the annual import requirement, according to a Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways reply in the Lok Sabha (S23). The Core quotes installed capacity of about 70,000 containers a year but production near 25,000 (S6), so estimates of current scale differ by source. China accounts for an estimated 85-97% of global dry-container production (S6, S7), and CIMC is the largest single producer (S6).

The CMPS goal is to raise India's annual container manufacturing capacity about ten-fold, to up to 7.5 lakh TEU, creating about 3,000 direct and over 50,000 indirect jobs (S2). A Rajya Sabha reply on 17 Mar 2026 showed the scheme, then called CMAS, was still at the appraisal stage (S23).

items: Indian-made containers cost an estimated $500-1,000 more than Chinese equivalents. A 40ft box would need to be made for about $2,400-2,450 to compete (Rohit Aggarwal, quoted in S6).
Outlook Business puts the gap at 30-40%, or $700-1,000 per container (S7).

Corten steel is about 60-65% of manufacturing cost. Indian corten is 10-15% dearer than Chinese, a $300-400 per box disadvantage. Specialised weathering steel is well under 1% of India's 125-130 mt of crude steel output (S6).
In the 2022 CONCOR order to Mazagon Dock, each domestic box was expected to cost about Rs 3.5-4 lakh (S15).

blocks.text: The brief's comparison of roughly Rs 1.5-2 lakh (China) versus Rs 3.5-4 lakh (India) per 40ft box could not be confirmed against a source for the China figure. Only the Indian Rs 3.5-4 lakh figure (2022, S15) and the dollar-gap estimates (S6, S7) are used here.

rows: Support on every container built to global shipping standards and sold by eligible makers
3% p.a. on eligible term loans for greenfield plants and brownfield expansion
Common facilities, e.g. dynamic longitudinal impact testing
Not explained in the release; land-leasing support was reported by some outlets but is not in the Cabinet release

blocks.title: CMPS outlay by component
blocks.source: Source: Cabinet approval as reported by Deccan Chronicle and Kashmir Despatch (S1, S2)

blocks.caption: Eligibility and per-unit parameters (as reported; guidelines not yet notified)
rows: S1; S4 notes this came from press reports, not the release text
At least 70% until FY32, at least 90% from FY33

items: Operational guidelines: per-container rates and eligibility rules are not stated in the Cabinet release, and no date has been given for guidelines (S4).

No exchange filing, board approval or rating rationale announcing a CMPS-linked 1 lakh TEU plant was found in searches covering 28-29 Oct 2026. DCM Shriram's Q2 FY27 announcements did not mention containers (S20).
The budget-stage scheme (Feb 2026) described a five-year period (S5). The approved CMPS runs to FY2039-40 (S2), giving a three-year build window followed by production support (S1, S3).

blocks.text: Scale check (our arithmetic): at the reported Rs 86,625 per 40ft box (S3), the Rs 8,891 cr opex pool would cover about 10 lakh 40ft boxes over the scheme life. A single 1 lakh TEU plant producing only 40ft boxes would make about 50,000 boxes a year.

blocks.caption: Listed names with company or primary evidence of container manufacturing
rows: 13,000+ containers since 2021 (S12); 10,000 TEU/yr capacity, container production at Shivlakha from Jun 2026 (S13)
Below the 25,000 TEU brownfield addition; earlier plan was 6,000 + 10,000 = 16,000 (S12, S14)
Built Maersk's first India-made EXIM box, unveiled at Dadri on 3 Jul 2026 (S24, S9); denied the reported 1,000-unit order on 6 Jul 2026 (S10)
CONCOR order for 2,500 steel boxes, about Rs 100 cr, May 2022 (S15)

items: BHEL: the government routed developmental orders for 1,000 containers each to BHEL and Braithwaite in Dec 2020, with prototypes to be tested first (S16). No later delivery evidence was found. Trade Brains still lists it as a beneficiary (S17).
Trans Freight Containers (BSE 513063) was named in a Feb 2026 'stocks to watch' list (S18). It has near-zero sales, and per Screener manufacturing has ceased with no plans to restart (S19).
Texmaco Rail and Titagarh Rail make container wagons, not boxes (S18). L&T and SCI are linked through ports and shipping, not manufacturing (S18).
CONCOR is a buyer: it imported about 10,000 containers a year from China around 2020 (S16) and placed the Mazagon order (S15). Its shares rose over 4% on the Budget announcement (S17).

blocks.text: Market-cap gap: confirmed box-making exposure sits in one micro/small cap (Kalyani), with no scheme-scale applicant named yet. For the large caps (DCM Shriram, Mazagon, BHEL), containers are immaterial to revenue on the evidence available.

items: Trade Brains (1 Feb 2026) named CONCOR, Kalyani Cast-Tech, BHEL and Mazagon Dock as likely beneficiaries. It cautioned that real benefits depend on implementation speed and orders, and it gave no container revenue figures (S17).
India Shipping News (7 Feb 2026) listed six 'stocks to watch'. Only one, Trans Freight, was a box maker, and it is dormant (S18, S19).
The Core (25 Feb 2026): experts called the Rs 10,000 cr outlay modest relative to global market dynamics, and warned of subsidy dependence, steel-mill reluctance and idle-capacity risk (S6).

Maersk: its global head of ocean assets partnerships said it needs 400,000-500,000 containers a year, and executives called the India order 'just the beginning' while saying sustained momentum needs the scheme (S8).
No sell-side initiating coverage dedicated to the CMPS theme was found. Coverage so far is media lists and investor forums.
Materiality: containers are a minor or unquantified line for DCM Shriram, Mazagon and BHEL (S15, S16, S20).
Guideline risk: per-unit rates and local-content rules come from a single report (S3). Thresholds come from press reports, not the release (S4).
Execution: three-year commissioning deadline (S1); corten supply and 70-90% local-content compliance (S3, S6).
Competition: China could cut prices further if India's scale-up lags (S6).
Order risk: DCM Shriram denied the headline Maersk order (S10); Kalyani's order book is Rs 133 cr against a Rs 170 cr+ goal (S13).
Valuation: Kalyani at Rs 1,153 trades at about 55x P/E on FY26 sales of Rs 150 cr (S11).

companies.name: Kalyani Cast-Tech Ltd
companies.role: Makes castings and specialised cargo containers (ISO 20/40ft, double-stack, special types) (S11). It has built 13,000+ containers since 2021 (S12) and runs 10,000 TEU/yr container and 2,400 wagon capacity at Shivlakha, Kutch, with a Gati Shakti cargo terminal (S13).
companies.impact: The only listed pure-play. To qualify as a CMPS brownfield expansion it must add at least 25,000 TEU (S4), about 2.5x its current capacity. The stock has already moved from Rs 439 to Rs 1,153 (S11).

companies.name: DCM Shriram Ltd
companies.role: Through group company DCM Shriram International, built India's first EXIM-grade box for Maersk, unveiled at Dadri on 3 Jul 2026 (S24, S9, S10).
companies.impact: The company denied the reported 1,000-unit Maersk order (S10) and has disclosed no container capacity or capex. On Rs 13,538 cr revenue, containers are not material yet (S20).

companies.name: Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Ltd
companies.role: Defence shipyard that took a May 2022 CONCOR order for 2,500 steel boxes worth about Rs 100 cr (S15).
companies.impact: Recent announcements make no mention of containers (S21). The scheme is immaterial against Rs 13,006 cr FY26 revenue unless it bids for a scheme-scale plant (S21).

companies.name: Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd
companies.role: Received a developmental order for 1,000 containers in Dec 2020 alongside Braithwaite (S16); described by Trade Brains as making ISO containers (S17).
companies.impact: No delivery or current container-line evidence was found. Treat it as an optional PSU candidate, not a confirmed participant (S16, S17).

companies.name: Jupiter Wagons Ltd
companies.role: Wagon maker whose portfolio includes ISO marine containers; reported growth in its container manufacturing segment in FY26 (S22).
companies.impact: A potential brownfield candidate with rail-fabrication scale. It has disclosed no container capacity or revenue split (S22).

companies.name: Container Corporation of India Ltd
companies.role: Rail container logistics operator and buyer of boxes: it imported about 10,000 a year from China (S16) and placed domestic orders with Mazagon Dock (S15).
companies.impact: Benefits as a buyer if domestic supply becomes price-competitive. Its shares rose over 4% on the Budget announcement (S17).

companies.name: Trans Freight Containers Ltd
companies.role: Former marine container maker named in Feb 2026 'container stocks' lists (S18).
companies.impact: Manufacturing has ceased and sales are near zero, with no plans to restart (S19). This is a media attribution without operating exposure.

companies.name: Texmaco Rail & Engineering Ltd
companies.role: Freight wagon maker named as a container-scheme 'stock to watch'; its exposure is container wagons, not boxes (S18).
companies.impact: Indirect at best: more domestic boxes do not change wagon demand directly (S18).

companies.name: Titagarh Rail Systems Ltd
companies.role: Wagon and rolling-stock maker named in the same list; its container link is container-movement equipment, not box-making (S18).

method: First edition, researched on 29 Oct 2026 from web searches and pages opened directly. Cabinet-approval details come from same-day news reports, because the PIB release page returned HTTP 403. Single-source items (per-unit support, local content) are flagged as such. Import and production baselines come from MoPSW parliamentary replies as cited by IMPRI. Company exposure was checked against Screener pages, company-linked news and the Feb 2026 media 'container stocks' lists. Names with only media attribution are labelled. Brief figures that could not be confirmed were left out: the Rs 1.5-2 lakh China box cost, Kalyani's 6,000-to-16,000 TEU status beyond the 2025 plan, and DCM Shriram's 1-year return. No ratings or price targets.

container_makers: Listed companies already building or expanding shipping/cargo container production in India
psu_fabricators: Large caps with a past or small container line, where it is a minor part of the business
